---
title: "Choices worth knowing about"
description: >
  Convergence, boundaries, starting values, units, the data rules and the priors of gibbs().
---

## Convergence

Convergence takes TWO things, not one. The step criterion is the RELATIVE change in the
components, `sqrt(sum(dtheta^2) / sum(theta^2)) < tol`, with a default of 1e-8: never an
absolute threshold on the score, which grows with the number of records. Coming from the
BLUPF90 family, mind the scale: those programs test that quantity squared, so a card's
`conv_crit` is this `tol` squared. A 1e-12 there is `tol = 1e-6` here, and the 1e-8
default here would be 1e-16 on that scale.

A small step is not an optimum, though. A damped step can accept a tiny move with the
gradient still far from zero, so `converged` also requires the NEWTON DECREMENT,
`g' AI^-1 g`, which is about twice the remaining gap in -2logL, to fall under 2e-4. It is
reported as `newton_dec`, next to `score`, so the certificate can be read rather than
trusted. Components resting at a covariance boundary are excluded from it, because a
component pinned there points out of the cone by construction and its gradient never
vanishes; when that happens the message says how many were excluded, and the
certification is conditional on that pinning.

## Covariance boundaries

In `model()` a component at its floor is excluded only when the score pushes it out of
the cone. In `model_mt()` the step freezes a boundary block whatever the sign, so the certificate is checked on the likelihood: points inside the cone along the
negative eigenvectors of the block's gradient, steps along the boundary face by finite
differences, and a second walk from inside the cone. A point that lowers the -2logL by
more than 1e-4 sends the walk there, or refuses the certificate when the walk cannot move.
Without those checks a real bivariate fit had been certified 46.8 units above its interior
optimum. A boundary face is flat, so a certified point is then polished along it while
each step gains more than 1e-5 and the point still certifies. In simulated sweeps of 368
fits from four starts per data set (run during development, not kept in `validation/`),
every certified point then came within 9.4e-5 of the best of its starts, and in a
separate search one pair of starts still certified points 1.7e-4 apart.

## How a fit ends

Two endings get their own verdict in `model()` and `model_mt()`. When `maxiter` runs out
with the Newton decrement already under tolerance (and, in `model_mt()`, the boundary
checks passed), the likelihood is flat along
some direction: the fit returns `converged = TRUE` and says so, because more iterations
would not choose a point on that ridge. When the average information is singular at the
end, the message says SINGULAR and names the components the data do not separate; their
standard errors are NaN, the reported point depends on `start=`, and only combinations of
them are estimable. That is the design speaking, and the answer is more information, a
simpler model, or a component held fixed. In `model_mt()`, a stop where
no damped step and no EM step improves the likelihood is never a certificate: the message
gives the iteration and the decrement. `maxiter = 0` evaluates the start and reports
`converged = FALSE` in both fitters.

## Where a fit starts, and in what units

`model()` starts from `var(y)`, so a run does not inherit a neighbour's answer by
accident. `model_mt()` starts from the univariate optimum of each trait with every covariance between traits at zero, the start one builds
by hand in BLUPF90 or ASReml. On real data a bivariate fit with an autoregressive residual
from `var(y)` had walked to
r = -1 and r = +1 and stopped 41.3 -2logL units above the optimum the univariate start
reached in 6 iterations. That was measured before the walk was standardized per trait and
before the boundary checks above, and with the current engine no simulated case is known
where the `var(y)` start fails. A variance that a univariate fit left at zero starts at 1%
of the `var(y)` start, and the univariate fits run to their own optimum whatever
`maxiter` is. When the fit from that start stalls without a certificate, the `var(y)`
start is fitted too, and `start_from` says which start the returned fit used. The default
rests on that one real case, and the univariate fits cost time: at 24 000 records, 1.1 to
1.6 times the `var(y)` start on the median of 3 runs when both reach the same optimum
(`validation/unit_shift_start_scale.R`).

The multi-trait fitter walks on each trait divided by the power of two just above its
standard deviation, and report in the original units. Neither the walk, nor the
singularity verdict, nor the standard errors depend on the unit a trait is recorded in.
`y1` and `0.01 * y1` give the same estimates up to the scale factors and the same -2logL
up to the Jacobian, and a power-of-two factor gives the same fit bit for bit. Components
resting at a boundary are the exception: when the data round differently they can move
along the flat face they rest on (up to 0.6% measured, with the -2logL equal within
2.5e-5 after the Jacobian).
`model()` gets the same invariance from a variance floor proportional to the variance of
`y`. The -2logL is formed from the residuals, so a constant added to `y` leaves it
unchanged to 3e-14 (relative).

When you do want a different start, `start=` takes one in `model()` and `model_mt()`
alike: to warm-start from a submodel, or to check that the optimum does not
depend on where the search began, which is the only direct evidence of a global optimum a
non-convex likelihood offers.

A covariance that stops being positive-definite ends the fit instead of being nudged back
into range, and a fit that did not converge says so in the print, in the message and in
the object.

## The data rules

The data rules are equally deliberate. An unknown genotype code becomes NA and is
imputed by the marker mean; it never becomes the zero genotype, which is a real
observation. An animal of the data missing from the pedigree, a maternal grandsire
included, enters as a founder with a warning that counts and names it, as renumf90 numbers
every animal with a record. An id that matches a pedigree line written another way (a trailing
space, the case, leading zeros) stops the fit with both spellings. A parent cited without
a line of its own is an error rather than a new founder.

## The priors of gibbs()

The priors of `gibbs()` depart from the software in the field, and each part of the
default was decided against the simulated validation behind it (`?gibbs`, under `prior`).
The Gibbs programs of BLUPF90 put flat priors on the variances unless `OPTION prior` gives
a proper one (Misztal, 2017; Masuda, 2026); the default inverse-Wishart of MCMCglmm, with
`nu = 0`, has the kernel of `prior = "jeffreys"` here, and its notes warn that it can leave
a chain stuck at zero (Hadfield, n.d.); JWAS and BGLR use proper scaled inverse-Wishart
priors (Cheng, Fernando and Garrick, 2018; Perez and de los Campos, 2014); brms puts a
half-t with 3 degrees of freedom on each standard deviation (Burkner, 2017). No
animal-breeding Gibbs program was found whose default is a hierarchical half-t. Here, left
unset: the half-t of Huang and Wand (2013) on each scalar random term, with its scale read
from the design, because on the scalar validation it had no chain stuck at a planted
variance of 0.05 (0 of 360) where `"jeffreys"` had 35 of 360, with coverage 171 of 180
against 160 of 180, and on an animal model of 2100 animals it landed beside REML (30 data
sets, with one record per animal and with two records and `pe()`); `"flat"` on each
covariance group, because `"jeffreys"` there holds chains at a
correlation of +-1 and the half-t, though it removed that trap, moved a direct-maternal correlation of -0.8 toward zero by 0.43 posterior SD; and
`"flat"` on the residual, which left the posterior of a scalar term where it was (it moves
`var(residual)` by the one degree of freedom that separates the two priors). A rule
written before the runs chose `"flat"`, and its clause on coverage did not say whose: read as that of the scalar term it passed, read as the residual's too it fails by one
data set in 120. Two sampler steps are on by default, both leaving the posterior
unchanged: the interweaving step of Yu and Meng (2011) on every estimated term of a
Gaussian trait and on each covariance group of a binary one, which raised the effective
sample size per iteration 5.2 to 10.6 times on covariance groups and 2.1 and 3.5 times on
scalar terms alone (pooled over the cases measured), and, on a binary trait, the PX-DA
move, on by a decision that overrides the rule written before the runs (keep a step only
if the lower 95% bound of its paired ESS ratio passes 1). Hobert and
Marchev (2008) prove Haar PX-DA at least as efficient as plain data augmentation for a
two-block chain, which covers the step between liabilities and locations here but not the
whole sweep. A plain proper inverse-Wishart was not the alternative: it inflates a variance
that sits below its scale and pulls correlations toward zero (Alvarez, Niemi and Simpson,
2014).
On a binary trait the half-t has df = 4 and, when a component is estimated, the fixed
effects of the liability a normal prior with standard deviation 1: with one binary record
per animal the likelihood stays positive as the variances grow, so a flat prior leaves the
posterior improper (Stock, Distl and Hoeschele, 2007, saw more than half of their threshold
runs fail under a flat prior on the genetic covariances; Odegard et al., 2010, saw the
standard sampler drift to an infinite variance), and with flat fixed effects so can a
half-t whose df does not exceed the number of fixed-effect columns. A proper
`c(df =, scale =)` is the scaled inverse chi-square of `OPTION prior` in the BLUPF90 Gibbs
programs; which prior those programs use without the option was not checked here.

## What the default prior does not do

What the default does not do: on one binary record per animal with 80 fixed classes, the design of Odegard et al. (2010), the default left 4 of 10 data sets at medians
of `var(animal)` of 15 to 62 after 4 chains of 25 000, against 0.25 planted (without `px`,
the same posterior, 3 of 10 at 11 to 49).

The works cited here by author and year are listed in full in the
[references](https://phyllype.github.io/UAI-TREM/REFERENCES.html).
